run_settings.records_only_directive:
## Staying inside your records
Say only what your own records hold. Every specific claim - a name, a date, a number, an event, a practice or a teaching - comes from one of your records and carries its [[record.id]] tag. Where your records do not hold what the question asks, say so plainly in your own voice, for example "our record does not say", rather than filling the gap. A shorter answer that stays inside your records is better than a fuller one that steps outside them.
run_settings.authorized_by: Mark Chadwick (keep going, 2026-10-03; fleet records-only check, cap $7)

off.answer_text:
We will answer this honestly, with what we actually have and with what we do not.

Someone who came to us came toward baptism. That much is plain - the font is everywhere in our hymns and letters, sung as a womb, as the place where believers are born a second time. Our own teacher said the believer receives the Holy Spirit in baptism's second birth. And he said something else, plainly: those who came were warned ahead of time. The preachers of the church were to tell them, before the water, what it would cost - that they were joining a people who carried a name, and that the name marked them out. That is the clearest witness we have to what happened before someone went into the font.

What we cannot give you is the step-by-step sequence. No order of worship survives from us - no manual, no teacher's letter laying out what came first and what came next. We can show you the pieces: the warning given beforehand, the font itself sung as the place of new birth, the sealing - the mark - set on each one who came up from the water. Every one of those pieces is real, attested in our own hymns and letters. But the sequence that held them together on an actual morning - who stood where, what was said in what order, how long it all took - our own record never wrote that down. We would rather hand you the pieces honestly than arrange them into a service we cannot show you.

And one thing more, just as honestly: the covenant stood at the center of our life. The sons and daughters of the covenant - the bnay and bnat qyama, the ihidaye, the Single Ones - took a vow of lifelong celibacy and service, and they remained inside the congregation, not away in the desert. Their choirs sang the teaching hymns in every church. How someone entered the covenant itself - whether before baptism or after, what words were said, whether there was a rite - our record does not say plainly enough for us to walk you through it. What we know is that the covenant was already established by the time our first datable letter addresses it. That letter corrects the covenant's practice; it does not found it. So the vow was real, public, and central - and the details of how it was entered are missing.

That is the honest answer: baptism as the door everyone came through, the covenant as the core some entered, and the sequence of either one kept only in pieces, not in order.

sources.spoken_rendering: For this reason it is right for the preachers of the Church - the ones who sound the trumpet - to warn everyone in God's covenant before baptism: those who choose for themselves virginity and holiness, the young men and the virgins, and those wishing to become holy. The preachers are to warn them and say this. If your heart is set on marriage, then marry before your baptism. Otherwise you may fall in the fight and be killed. And if you are afraid of this part of the fight, turn back now, so that you do not break your brothers' hearts along with your own. And if you love your possessions, turn back from the army too - or else, when the battle goes against you, you may remember your possessions and turn back to them, for there is disgrace for the one who turns back from the fight.
sources.speaker: Aphrahat, Demonstration VII.20

uncited_claim_sentences: Our own teacher said the believer receives the Holy Spirit in baptism's second birth.
That is the clearest witness we have to what happened before someone went into the font.
That letter corrects the covenant's practice; it does not found it.
So the vow was real, public, and central - and the details of how it was entered are missing.
That is the honest answer: baptism as the door everyone came through, the covenant as the core some entered, and the sequence of either one kept only in pieces, not in order.

records_only.answer_text:
We can tell you what the record holds - and we will tell you honestly where it runs thin.

The first step anyone took toward us was hearing. Someone taught the Gospel, and someone else listened - in a household, in the street, wherever the word traveled. What drew people in was the story itself: the one continuous Gospel we read, the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete, the harmony that made the four accounts into one telling. The faith reached them as a woven story, not as separate books.

Before baptism, we warned them what the promises would cost. Our own teacher says plainly: it is right for the preachers of the church to warn those who come to baptism of the contests ahead, so that when the contests come they will not flee. We cannot tell you how long that warning time lasted, or what order it followed on a given morning. What we kept was the fact of warning, not the schedule.

Baptism itself was sung as a second birth. The water was a womb. The believer went down into it and came up wearing new garments, shining, with the sign - the sealing - set on them. And in that second birth they received the Holy Spirit. Our hymns carried all of this, step by step, as the congregation sang the new believer into the covenant of the name. No ritual handbook survives to tell us what the presbyter said first, or where people stood, or in what exact order the words and the water came. We can show you the pieces - the font, the garments, the sealing. The sequence that bound them on an actual morning, our record never wrote down.

After baptism they belonged. They gathered with us on the first day of the week. They kept the fasts we kept. And some of them went further. Some took the vow of the qyama, the covenant: a lifelong promise to remain celibate and to serve. These were the ihidaye, the Single Ones - bnay qyama and bnat qyama, sons and daughters of the covenant. They did not leave for the desert. They stayed in town, among their own kin, and took on the vigil, the fast, the watch, and the work. Our teacher wrote to them in his sixth letter, already addressing them as established - a discipline in the middle of its own life, being corrected more than being founded. He told them to visit the Lord in the persons of the sick. That was the shape of their joining: a vow taken, a life changed, and work to do right where they already lived.

How exactly the vow was taken - before whom, in what words, at what moment in the year - we cannot tell you. The vow itself is real and plainly attested. The ceremony that made it binding is not described.

That is what we can show you: hearing, warning, baptism, belonging, and for some the vow. Where the record does not reach further, we name that plainly and leave the silence standing.

uncited_claim_sentences: The first step anyone took toward us was hearing.
Baptism itself was sung as a second birth.
And in that second birth they received the Holy Spirit.
They gathered with us on the first day of the week.
They kept the fasts we kept.
And some of them went further.
They did not leave for the desert.
That was the shape of their joining: a vow taken, a life changed, and work to do right where they already lived.
The ceremony that made it binding is not described.
Where the record does not reach further, we name that plainly and leave the silence standing.
